title: Impact of Irrep Truncations on Quantum Simulations of QCD
abstract: Quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories with continuous gauge groups require a choice of basis (how states of the gauge theory map to the qubit computational basis) and truncation scheme (which of the infinitely many gauge theory basis states should be omitted in the map to the finite dimensional qubit Hilbert space.) The most common choices are adapted to an electric basis for the gauge theory, where the basis states for each link are associated with irreducible representations of the gauge group. Electric bases and truncations are generally advantageous for preserving gauge symmetries and simulating the strong coupling regime, but their effectiveness in the weak coupling regimes of physical interest are less well understood. In this work, we compute relative probabilities $p(R')/p(R)$ for finding a link in the irreps $R,R'$ in the ground state of SU(3) lattice gauge theory using Euclidean Monte Carlo methods and weak-coupling lattice perturbation theory. The observables that compute these relative probabilities are constructed by introducing seams into an anisotropic lattice, and by a similar construction we are also able to measure relative probabilities of different site singlets (ways that electric flux braids together into a gauge singlet) at each vertex. With these methods we can quantify, for example, the importance of higher electric flux states in the weak coupling ground state. These results directly inform what truncations are needed to accurately capture non-abelian gauge dynamics near the continuum limit.
summary: This paper investigates how to accurately simulate lattice gauge theories like QCD on quantum computers by determining the necessary basis truncations. Using Monte Carlo and perturbation theory, the authors calculate the relative probabilities of different gauge field configurations (irreps and singlets). These results directly guide the construction of efficient quantum circuits for simulating non-abelian gauge dynamics.
main_problem: The core problem is determining the necessary truncation scheme when mapping the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space of lattice gauge theories onto a finite-dimensional qubit space for quantum simulation.
main_result: The study computes relative probabilities of link irreps and site singlets, providing quantitative data to inform the required truncation level needed to accurately capture non-abelian gauge dynamics near the continuum limit.
method: The authors employ Euclidean Monte Carlo methods and weak-coupling lattice perturbation theory to calculate these relative probabilities.
model_or_system: The system studied is SU(3) lattice gauge theory, analyzed using the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian framework.
key_observables: Relative probabilities of link irreps ($p(R')/p(R)$) and relative probabilities of different site singlets at each vertex.
important_parameters: Weak coupling regime ($g 	o 0$), anisotropic lattice limit ($\xi = a_s/a_t$), and the lattice spacing $a$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the gauge theory can be effectively described by an electric basis, although the effectiveness of this basis in weak coupling is questioned.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the ratio of the two-point collinear correlator calculated in lattice vs. continuum PT, showing agreement at large separations ($r/a \gtrsim 10$).
paper_structure: The work involves calculating observables (link irrep probabilities, site-singlet probabilities) using Monte Carlo methods and comparing these results against predictions from weak-coupling lattice perturbation theory.
why_interesting: The techniques used for calculating correlation functions and determining necessary basis truncations are highly relevant to simulating complex quantum many-body systems on quantum hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Active link irreps in Monte Carlo sampling of the seamed lattice at (a) β = 6.0 (g = 1) and (b) β = 7.089 (g = 0.92) for the heat kernel action at ξ = 5.0. The dots in the blue shaded region denote the irreps with character expectation values greater than 10−2 in every run of the MCMC. The characters with magnitude less than 10−2 cannot be measured reliably because the signal is overpowered by statistical noise.

Figure 3: Each panel plots the binned averages with bin size of 100 as a function of measure- ment index for irreps 3 + ¯3 and 27 for the following cases (β = 6.0 in all cases) – (a) Wilson action with ξ = 4.0; (b) heat kernel action with ξ = 4.0; (c) Wilson action with ξ = 5.0; and (d) heat kernel action with ξ = 5.0.
Figure 4: Jackknife errors plotted as a function of bin size plotted for ξ ≥3.0 with β = 6.0 for the Wilson and heat kernel actions for irreps 3 + ¯3 and 27.

Figure 5: Mean distributions plotted for different chains of the Wilson and heat kernel actions with ξ = 4.0 and β = 6.0 for irreps 3 + ¯3 using bootstrap sampling wherein N random samples are drawn with replacement 1000 times (N is the number of elements in the original sample space) and the mean is computed for each draw. Panels (a) and (c) plot the mean distributions of the heat kernel and Wilson actions without binning, and panels (b) and (d) plot the mean distributions of said actions after binning in bin sizes of 20 and 10.
